results.title: IRB SOP Investigator: Privacy and Confidentiality
results.content: o Methods used to transmit and code or de-identify the research data o Length of research data storage o Timeline and manner of destruction of research data IRB SOP Investigator: Privacy and Confidentiality NUMBER APPROVED BY EFFECTIVE DATE HSR-340 Miranda van Tilburg, PhD IRB Chair, IRB Office Campbell University 12/02/2020 Version: 2.0 Page 3 of 7 • If obtaining the Social Security Numbers (SSN) of research subjects, the PI’s plan for protecting privacy and confidentiality must also include the following information, at a minimum: o Justification for obtaining Social Security numbers o A statement in the Informed Consent document or other documents provided to research subjects explaining how SSN will be used such as in long-term follow-up for survival or for compensation o Whether Social Security numbers will be shared with parties outside of the institution o The method in which Social Security numbers will be stored o When and how Social Security numbers will be destroyed The names of research subjects, Social Security numbers, and payments should be kept in a secure place separate from the research data, subject files, and source documents.

results.title: Euclid Data Release Timeline | Euclid
results.content: * March 19, 2025: Quick Data Release 1 (Q1). **Future data releases with known dates:**. * June 24, 2026: Quick Data Release 2 (Q2). * October 21, 2026: Data Release 1 (DR1). * March 2029: Data Release 2 (DR2). * October 2031: Data Release 3 (DR3). **Data release plan** (click here for the most up-to-date Euclid data release timeline from ESA):. * Three main data releases (DR1, DR2, DR3), phased with the survey progress, with the final DR3 a year after the end of the main survey. ESA will release well characterized and validated data to the world wide community in each of the major Data Releases and Quick releases. The main component of the Q1 data contains Level 2 data of a single visit (at the depth of the Euclid Wide Survey) over the Euclid Deep Fields (EDFs): 20 deg2 of the EDF North, 10 deg2 of EDF Fornax, and 23 deg2 of the EDF South.

results.content: You can see from the example above that Numpy's RNG behaves the same way as Python's RNG: once a seed is set, the generator outputs the very same sequence of numbers, 6, 3, 7, and 4. But, it turns out, even though Numpy's legacy code and Python's random module use the same algorithm, and we're using the same seed in both of them, the generated numbers are *still* different! PyTorch can actually take care of itself in the above situation — it seeds each worker with a different number, that is, `base_seed + worker_id`, but it cannot take care of other packages (e.g. Numpy or Python's random module). Now every worker will use a different seed for PyTorch, Numpy, and Python's random module. Maybe you don't, but it's better to **play safe and set seeds for everything: PyTorch, Numpy, and even Python's random module**, and that's what we did in the previous section. results.title: Privacy Preserving Synthetic Data Release Using Deep Learning | Harvard Kennedy School
results.content: # Privacy Preserving Synthetic Data Release Using Deep Learning. ### HKS Authors. See citation below for complete author information. Over the years, data anonymization and synthetic data generation techniques have been proposed to address this challenge. Although, there are existing synthetic data generation techniques that use rigorous definitions of differential privacy, to our knowledge, these techniques have not been compared extensively using different utility metrics. Second, we present a novel approach that utilizes deep learning techniques coupled with an efficient analysis of privacy costs to generate differentially private synthetic datasets with higher data utility. We show that we can learn deep learning models that can capture relationship among multiple features, and then use these models to generate differentially private synthetic datasets. "Privacy Preserving Synthetic Data Release Using Deep Learning." *Machine Learning and Knowledge Discovery in Databases* (2018): 510-526.
